name: Reciprocity Norms
summary: The universal social expectation that gifts, favours, and obligations will be returned — the invisible protocol that makes trust, exchange, and cooperation possible without enforcement.

claims.statement: Reciprocity is documented in every known human society; Mauss demonstrated that gift exchange creates binding social obligations that predate and underpin all formal economic systems

Experimental economics confirms that humans enforce reciprocity norms even at personal cost (ultimatum games, public goods games), indicating these norms are not merely cultural but deeply embedded in human cognition

Indirect reciprocity (helping strangers because reputation circulates) scales cooperation beyond kin and small groups, enabling the large-scale societies that all other keystone technologies depend on

evidence.source: Mauss (1925) Essai sur le don (The Gift), L'Année Sociologique; English trans. Routledge 1990
Fehr & Gächter (2000) Fairness and Retaliation: The Economics of Reciprocity, Journal of Economic Perspectives 14(3)
Nowak & Sigmund (2005) Evolution of Indirect Reciprocity, Nature 437(7063)

notes: Resolves 1 inbound link from gift_economy. This is arguably the most fundamental social technology — the one without which none of the others function. Discounted in modern economics because it is invisible, unpriced, and omnipresent. Mauss's insight: the gift is never free, it is the original social contract.
